text: I did some experiments on using the Closure API for compressing code remotely. You just gather the code to compress (as we do in the build.py script right now), and post it to their endpoint, then grab the compressed results if all went fine. It's somethin"
body:
I did some experiments on using the Closure API for compressing code remotely. You just gather the code to compress (as we do in the build.py script right now), and post it to their endpoint, then grab the compressed results if all went fine. It's something like this:

``` python
def get_response(data):
    post_data = urllib.parse.urlencode(data)
    request = urllib.request.Request('http://closure-compiler.appspot.com/compile', post_data.encode())
    response = urllib.request.urlopen( request )

    compressed = response.read()

    return compressed

values = {
    'compilation_level': 'SIMPLE_OPTIMIZATIONS',
    'output_format': 'text',
    'output_info': 'compiled_code',
    'js_code': string
}

compressed_js = get_response( values )

if len(compressed_js) == 1:
    print('BOOOH ERRORS FOUND!!!')
    values['output_info'] = 'errors'

    errors = get_response( values )
    print(errors)

else:

    with open(outfile, 'wb') as f:
        f.write(compressed_js)

```

My bad, I reverted my changes, rebuilt and now I see it (Lucy has strongest effect). Must have been some caching issue.

> By the way, I'm a bit confused with the ratio the refraction uses. 
> But the material seem to use another range?

These are indices of refraction, specific for one material (IOR). Refraction ratio is IOR1 / IOR2 when light passes between two materials. 

For example:

```
 air / water => 1.0003 / 1.3333 ~= 0.75
 air / glass => 1.0003 / 1.5 ~= 0.67
```

There is some problem, though, for inversed ratios (e.g. air bubble inside water), there are some artefacts around object edges :(. Don't know what's expected behavior for such cases (with this particular implementation).

Microsoft managed to get better results from coevolving GPU hardware, despite developers gnashing their teeth. Ultimately what mattered was that end users were getting cooler games on DirectX (even with such titans as John Carmack being for a long time firmly in OpenGL camp).
